source.title: Quantifying construct validity in large language model evaluations

record.file_problem: None noted; the full thesis text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream benchmark-score predictability with observational leaderboard data and out-of-fold prediction, rather than measuring the original held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study uses and compares scaling-law approaches, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss, sweep training tokens or compute, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own relevant results are logistic fits of BBH scores against parameter size and held-out BBH prediction errors. The cited Kaplan, Hoffmann and Ruan findings are background, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study tests V6 by fitting BBH performance against parameter count and evaluating parameter-based predictions on the highest-scoring 20% of models. Its benchmark-to-benchmark capability predictions address a different question. It does not test pretraining-loss laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: The author argues that combining model scale with latent-factor measurement improves capability estimation: structured models have better AIC/BIC than corresponding unstructured models, and SC has lower average held-out prediction error than OSL. Qualifications: adding the structural size term worsens absolute fit indices within each data representation, and SC’s average prediction advantage is not statistically significant (test p = 0.637).
record.recipe_differences: Uses logistic fits of benchmark accuracy and capability models on leaderboard results, not the original neural-language-model cross-entropy measurements or compute-allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction errors vary by held-out BBH subtask and by capability-estimation method. Across the 19 tasks, SC has lower test MSE than OSL on 12; the average test-MSE difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.637). The text also reports logistic parameter-size score-fit R2 values from 0.12 (Web of lies) to 0.52 (Ruin names).

fits_no_version.finding: SC and PCA-derived capabilities predict one BBH subtask using scores on the other 18. Average test MSE is 1.156 versus 1.473; the difference is nonsignificant (p = 0.637). These are capability-estimation method comparisons, not direct demonstrations of improvement with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark-derived capability representations can predict performance on other benchmark tasks; explicitly modelling measurement error may improve generalisation.

record.problems: Only one benchmark family (BBH) is analyzed, with multiple-choice evaluation; the authors caution that findings may not generalize to open-ended tasks or real-world scenarios. The SC versus OSL average prediction advantage is not statistically significant (p = 0.637). The analysis is observational, not causal. The logistic score-fit R2 values range from 0.12 to 0.52.
record.rows_left_out: The study also reports training-set MSE for all 19 tasks and per-task logistic parameter-size fit results (Appendix E / Figure 13). These were not extracted because the 60-row cap was reached after retaining test-set MSE by task and the aggregate test errors. Training-set results are in Table 3; the figure-based fit range and examples are described in Results §4.1 and Appendix E, Figure 13.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and its power-law dependence on parameters, tokens or compute.
Small-run power-law prediction of pretraining loss at orders-of-magnitude larger scales.
Fixed-compute optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling exponents.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.
Prediction from pretraining loss, training tokens or compute; controlled within-family scaling; extrapolation to larger parameter counts; downstream domains beyond multiple-choice BBH.
Dependence of power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices; departures from a single power-law loss curve.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 3 numbers match the supplied text. Their targets are transformed scores B′, not raw accuracy, and the split selects the bottom/top portions of held-out task performance, not parameter size. The 4,395 models form the full sample rather than the test set alone. SC and OSL also use the test models’ other benchmark scores. Nonzero MSE alone does not justify a partial state or show absent scaling. The direct size-fit R² results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing; the V6 qualification rests explicitly on those textual results. Differences between SC and OSL do not independently limit V6 or test V7.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or power-law dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
Does not fit pretraining-loss power laws on small runs and test extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute training experiments or parameter/token allocation is examined.
Does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer are studied.
Tests prediction of BBH benchmark accuracy from leaderboard benchmark data and parameter size, not the general downstream-task relationship to pretraining loss or other task domains.

Although the study compares capability-estimation methods and a logistic benchmark-score model, it does not test whether neural pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with setup, nor whether loss curves bend from a power law.
